subject: astronomy

moments.title: Schwarzschild solution
moments.body: Months after Einstein publishes general relativity, German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild — serving in the German artillery on the Eastern Front — produces the first exact solution to Einstein's field equations. The solution implies an event horizon at r = 2GM/c². Schwarzschild dies of a skin disease (pemphigus) months later, before seeing his work published.
moments.takeaway: The mathematics of black holes was worked out in the trenches of WWI by a man who would not live to see his work in print.

moments.title: First image of a black hole (M87*)
moments.body: On 10 April 2019, the EHT releases the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole at the centre of M87, mass ~6.5 billion suns, 55 million light years away. The image combines data from 8 radio telescopes across the globe — a virtual telescope the size of Earth. Katie Bouman's image-reconstruction algorithm becomes famous.
moments.takeaway: An image we were told was impossible was made by combining data from telescopes on four continents.

moments.title: Sgr A* imaged
moments.body: On 12 May 2022, the EHT releases the image of Sgr A*, the 4-million-solar-mass black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. Imaging Sgr A* is harder than M87 because it varies on shorter timescales.
moments.takeaway: We have directly imaged the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy.

now.title: Black holes today
now.body: EHT is expanding (next-generation EHT). Hawking radiation (1974) remains theoretically predicted but undetected. The information paradox (does information escape black holes?) remains contested. JWST has found supermassive black holes at high redshift larger than formation models predict.
now.open_questions: How did supermassive black holes grow so large so fast in the early universe? Direct-collapse origin or rapid accretion?

reflection: Karl Schwarzschild's son Martin became a leading 20th-century astrophysicist at Princeton. Black holes — Schwarzschild's mathematics — were imaged by another generation entirely. Discoveries outlive their discoverers in ways that lesser work does not.
